content: A Cochrane systematic review has demonstrated that treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnant women with antibiotics significantly reduces the risk of developing pyelonephritis and lowers the likelihood of preterm delivery. However, it remains uncertain whether a single-dose antibiotic regimen is as effective as a longer, conventional course of treatment. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of different durations of antibiotic treatment for asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy. Researchers conducted a search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of August 31, 2015) and reviewed reference lists of relevant articles. The study included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared antimicrobial regimens of varying durations, specifically single-dose treatments versus short-course regimens lasting four to seven days, in pregnant women diagnosed with asymptomatic bacteriuria. Two independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, extracted data, and verified the accuracy of the findings. The quality of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Thirteen studies involving a total of 1,622 pregnant women were included in the analysis. All studies compared single-dose antibiotic treatments with short-course regimens lasting four to seven days. The risk of bias in the included trials was generally unclear, with many studies showing a high risk of performance bias. The quality of evidence was graded using the GRADE system. When any antibiotic agent was used, the rate of no cure for asymptomatic bacteriuria was slightly lower with short-course treatments compared to single-dose treatments. However, there was significant statistical heterogeneity in the results (average risk ratio [RR] 1.28, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.87 to 1.88; 1,502 women; 13 studies; I² = 56%; very low-quality evidence). Data from higher-quality trials showed that short-course regimens of the same antibiotic agent were more effective in achieving a cure (average RR 1.72, 95% CI 1.27 to 2.33; 803 women; two studies; I² = 0%; high-quality evidence). There was no clear difference in the recurrence rate of asymptomatic bacteriuria between treatment groups, regardless of whether the same or different microbial agents were used (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.66; 445 women; eight studies; I² = 0%; very low-quality evidence). However, a single trial showed that short-course regimens were associated with a lower risk of delivering low birthweight babies (RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.57; 714 women; high-quality evidence). No significant differences were observed between treatment groups for preterm delivery (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.78; 804 women; three studies; I² = 23%; moderate-quality evidence) or pyelonephritis (RR 3.09, 95% CI 0.54 to 17.55; 102 women; two studies; I² = 0%; very low-quality evidence). Single-dose antibiotic regimens were associated with fewer reports of side effects compared to short-course treatments (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.88; 1,460 women; 12 studies; I² = 9%; low-quality evidence). The evidence was downgraded due to concerns about bias in the contributing trials and imprecise effect estimates, which included wide confidence intervals and, in some cases, small sample sizes with few events. In conclusion, single-dose antibiotic regimens may be less effective than short-course regimens lasting four to seven days. However, further research is needed, particularly large trials that measure critical outcomes such as cure rates. Until more robust data are available, pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria should be treated with the standard antibiotic regimen. Future studies should also explore the efficacy of shorter courses, such as threeor five-day regimens, compared to the standard seven-day treatment.
